title: A posted cannabis script
problemType: Legally valid but possibly not clinically appropriate (high-risk medicine)
questionSheet: A patient presents a prescription for a medicinal cannabis product, written by a prescriber in a different city in the same state. He tells you he had a telehealth appointment and the prescription was posted to him. He says it is for his mental health, but gives no further details. Manage the situation as you would in practice. You may contact the prescriber.

prescription.item: Medicinal cannabis oral oil, THC 10 mg/mL + CBD 10 mg/mL
prescription.directions: 0.25 mL at night, increase as directed · Qty 1 × 25 mL
prescription.footer: Telehealth prescriber, Sydney · Posted to patient

notes: Schedule 8 medicine: NSW requirements for dispensing apply.

patient.label: Patient · Mr D
patient.name: Mr D
patient.description: A man in his twenties, polite but guarded. Keeps answers short and changes the subject when asked about his health. Becomes uncomfortable if pressed hard, but answers direct, respectful questions, especially when the pharmacist explains why they need to know.
patient.openingLine: Hi, I need this filled please.
publicFacts: He had a telehealth appointment with the prescriber.
The prescription was posted to him.
If asked what it is for, he says it's for his mental health and doesn't want to go into it.

prescriber.label: Call the prescriber
prescriber.name: Dr Lane
prescriber.description: A telehealth prescriber in another city. Professional and a little defensive about their prescribing. Responds well to a respectful, specific question about the indication and history, and poorly to vague criticism.
prescriber.openingLine: Dr Lane speaking. You're calling about one of my patients?
publicFacts: You wrote the prescription after a telehealth consultation and posted it to the patient.

hiddenFacts.fact: This is your first prescription for it. You've never used medicinal cannabis before.
hiddenFacts.unlockHint: “Is this the first time you've been prescribed this?”

hiddenFacts.fact: It's for anxiety and trouble sleeping.
hiddenFacts.unlockHint: “I'm asking so I can make sure it's safe for you. What symptoms is it meant to help with?”

hiddenFacts.fact: Your older brother has schizophrenia. Nobody asked you about that at the appointment.
hiddenFacts.unlockHint: “Does anyone in your family have a history of mental illness, such as psychosis?”

hiddenFacts.fact: You prescribed it for generalised anxiety disorder with insomnia. He tried sertraline for six weeks last year and stopped it because of nausea. He hasn't had any psychological therapy.
hiddenFacts.unlockHint: “What's the indication, and what treatments has he tried before?”

hiddenFacts.fact: You didn't ask about personal or family history of psychosis. You're willing to review the prescription if there is a risk.
hiddenFacts.unlockHint: “Did you screen for a personal or family history of psychosis? His brother has schizophrenia.”

answerKey.plantedProblem: A legally valid prescription that may not be clinically appropriate. Evidence for medicinal cannabis in anxiety and depression is lacking, and THC-containing products may be contraindicated in some mental health conditions such as psychosis. Here there is a family history of schizophrenia and no first-line therapy has been tried properly.
acceptableResolutions: Gather his history, diagnosis, current symptoms and treatment goals respectfully, explaining why it matters.
Withhold supply until the prescriber is contacted to confirm the indication and history, and that benefits outweigh risks. The decision to supply stays with the pharmacist.
Raise the concerns (family history of psychosis, weak evidence, first-line options) with the prescriber respectfully and collaboratively.
Explain the concerns to him in clear, appropriate language.
If dispensing, counsel on adverse effects, warning signs needing review, driving and when to stop, and reassess at each dispensing.
If declining, help him access a suitable healthcare professional.
Document the reasoning, decision and actions, and comply with NSW Schedule 8 requirements.
unacceptableActions: Refusing without speaking to the prescriber or arranging alternative care.
legal: NSW requirements for dispensing Schedule 8 medicines, including checking the prescription and real-time prescription monitoring.
answerKey.modelAnswer: The prescription is legally valid but may not be clinically appropriate. Gather his diagnosis, history, symptoms and goals: here, anxiety and insomnia, no prior cannabis use, and a brother with schizophrenia. The dilemma is acting in his best interests while avoiding harm with a high-risk medicine that lacks strong evidence. Don't supply until you've spoken to the prescriber about the indication, previous treatments and the family history of psychosis; the decision to supply remains yours. Communicate concerns clearly to him and collaboratively with the prescriber. If supplying, counsel and reassess at each dispensing; if not, help him access appropriate care. Document everything and follow S8 requirements.
